sections.html:
Chaves County's seat, Roswell, stands at about 3,615 feet some 7 miles west of the Pecos River. Its 48,422 residents in 2020 made it the fifth largest city in the state, and because the county is the entire micropolitan area, Roswell is where people go for shopping, health care and county offices. US 70, 285 and 380 meet in town.

Most Roswell buyers live nearby already. Irrigated farms, dairies, factories such as the Leprino Foods mozzarella plant, a military institute and college campuses all feed that local pool, which is smaller than a big metro's and tends to move at its own pace.

sections.h2: Older houses and what buyers ask
sections.html:
The town dates to 1871 and incorporated in 1889, so plenty of its houses are old. Lenders and buyers often ask about original wiring, plumbing and heating. Cash buyers usually accept those as they are, while a financed purchase may come with repair conditions.

Any roof replacement, plumbing update or electrical upgrade deserves a saved receipt. Dates and paperwork answer an inspector's first questions.

sections.h2: Weather and the Rio Hondo flood history
sections.html:
Four distinct seasons shape a cold semi-arid climate, with 11.63 inches of precipitation and 9.6 inches of snow in a typical year. Daily highs average 56.5 degrees in December and 96.5 in July, and the record range is minus 24 to 114, so a buyer cares about both heating and cooling. Monsoon storms bring downpours, severe thunderstorms and, at times, tornadoes.

The Rio Hondo has flooded here before. Mass flooding in 1937, 1941 and 1954 led to a flood control facility at Two Rivers Dam, and the city posts FEMA flood information showing changes to the Hondo River floodplains.

  • Look up the address on the FEMA flood map before listing.
  • Ask your insurance agent about a mapped floodplain.
  • Save records of any roof, drainage or storm repair.

Roswell's Code Enforcement Department looks after neighborhood upkeep. Municipal Code section 16-12 lets the City Council declare structures dangerous buildings and public nuisances. Empty, damaged or neglected houses can draw a complaint ahead of any sale, so settle open notices first.

Applications, email updates and inspection requests for residential permits all go through an online system. Find out from the city whether earlier work at your address was permitted, because a lender may ask for proof.

Property tax for Roswell addresses runs through Chaves County, and the proceeds are shared among the State of New Mexico, the county, Roswell Independent School District, ENMU-Roswell, the City of Roswell and the Flood Control Conservancy District.

Find the Assessor at 1 St Mary's Place or call the county's main line, 575-624-6600. Protest a value within 30 days after the Notice of Value is mailed.

Two years of unpaid tax, penalty and interest send the records to the State Property Tax Division, with a $125 cost to state fee and a risk of public auction. Counties hold that auction yearly in their commission chambers.

A lien attaches on January 1 of the tax year, and whoever owns the house of record that day is responsible for that year. When a sale happens in spring, the contract normally divides the current year between the two sides, and the closing statement should show exactly how.

sections.h2: What to gather before talking to a buyer
sections.html:
One folder of documents helps every kind of sale.

  • The newest Chaves County tax bill, with proof of payment for both halves.
  • Any code enforcement notice, with its date and what it asked you to fix.
  • Receipts or permits for roof, plumbing, heating or storm repairs.
  • Your address's FEMA flood zone and any flood policy.
  • If inherited: the death certificate plus probate or title papers.

Having them ready means a buyer can quote you sooner and nothing catches you off guard at closing.

A house left empty after an owner passes tends to attract attention. Neighbors notice tall weeds and a quiet yard, and the city can act on a structure it considers dangerous. If you inherited a Roswell house, first confirm who has legal authority to sell. That usually means probate or clear title paperwork. Then walk the property, photograph its condition, and look for any city notice taped to a door.

Roof leaks and frozen pipes are the usual damage in an empty house here, since winters get cold and storms can be hard. Turning off water and covering known leaks costs little compared with a damaged ceiling. Tell any buyer what you found, because honest disclosure keeps a cash sale from stalling.

After you accept an offer, the title company opens the file and checks ownership, liens and tax. It asks the county for a payoff figure on any balance and prepares a closing statement showing who pays what. You review that statement, sign the deed and settlement papers, and hand over the keys. Proceeds arrive after the mortgage, liens and the tax split are paid.

Delays usually come from missing paperwork, not from the buyer. A death certificate, a probate order, a lost deed or an unreleased old mortgage can add days. Gather those items first and ask the title company to list anything still needed. A clear checklist is the best way to keep the date.

Set expectations early. A cash offer is typically lower than what a fully repaired house might bring through a listing, and the difference pays for speed and certainty. Ask each buyer how they arrived at the number, whether the offer changes after an inspection, and who pays title and closing costs. A buyer who answers plainly and puts the terms in writing is easier to trust than one who stays vague. Compare offers on the amount you would actually receive, not on the headline price alone.

Listing, selling directly and taking a cash offer are the three paths, and condition, timing and cost decide among them.

  • Listing: puts the house in front of the most buyers, while repairs, showings and closing costs land on you.
  • Direct sale: skips an agent but you set the price and draft the paperwork.
  • Cash offer: a buyer takes the house as-is. Get it in writing and read every term.

Cash tends to appeal for inherited houses, vacant properties with code notices, flood or storm repair, tenants, and taxes that have slipped. On any route, find out from the title company how taxes and liens are paid at closing.

faqs.a: Roswell is in Chaves County and is its county seat. Chaves County forms the entire Roswell micropolitan area.

faqs.q: When are Chaves County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Mailing is by November 1. The first half is due November 10 and delinquent December 11, and the second half is due April 10 and delinquent May 11.

faqs.q: Is Roswell at risk of flooding?
faqs.a: Parts of it have been. The Rio Hondo caused mass flooding in 1937, 1941 and 1954, and a flood control facility followed. Check FEMA flood information for your address.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not pay Roswell property taxes?
faqs.a: At two years unpaid, the records go to the State Property Tax Division with a $125 cost to state fee, and public auction becomes possible.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Roswell house without making repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. Cash buyers take the house as-is, or you can list and negotiate after inspection. Weigh your net on each.
